# OPERATION — jarvis_os

This project is managed by **Jarvis**, the agentic OS. This file is the operating
contract every agent working here must follow.

## How work arrives

1. Work orders are created via `jarvis wo create jarvis_os "..."`, the Jarvis web
   UI, or (discouraged) direct insert into `.jarvis/jarvis.db`.
2. The Jarvis daemon polls this project's queue (`.jarvis/jarvis.db`, gitignored) and
   spawns one Claude Code background worker per work order, in a fresh git worktree.
3. The worker owns the work order end to end. It may brainstorm, invoke skills, spawn
   subagents, or run workflows — its call. It works autonomously toward a complete
   solution unless the work order says otherwise.

## Worker obligations

While handling work order `$JARVIS_WO_ID`, you MUST:

- **Work in your assigned worktree** (you are started in it). Commit your work; push
  and open a PR following this repo's conventions. Never push to main.
- **Title the PR `[$JARVIS_WO_ID] <what it does>`** — the work order id verbatim, in
  square brackets, first. That prefix is what ties the pull request back to the work
  order for everyone who never sees Jarvis, so `gh pr create` with any other title is
  blocked by the hook.
- **Route any doubt to Neo — it is your first responder**:
  `jarvis wo ask "$JARVIS_WO_ID" "<your question>"`, then end your turn.

  The answer arrives as your next user turn, usually within a minute, from Neo (the
  user's delegate) or the user. This is the *normal, expected* way to work: it is not
  an escalation, it does not interrupt the user, and it costs you about a minute. Put
  everything needed to decide inside the question text — whoever answers sees only
  that text, never your session — with the concrete options and your recommendation.

  The trigger is **doubt**, not importance. If you catch yourself weighing options,
  thinking "either would work", or picking one because you have to pick something, you
  are in doubt: ask, *before* you build on it.

  Do not talk yourself out of asking. "It's reversible", "it's only an implementation
  detail", "I'll note it as an assumption" — those are rationalisations for guessing.
  Almost everything is reversible; that is not the question. The question is whether
  you would be *rebuilding* if you guessed wrong.
- **Record the calls you were sure about** — this should be rare:
  `jarvis wo assume "$JARVIS_WO_ID" "<the assumption>"`

  An assumption is for the *other* case: a call you made with **no doubt** — you
  followed an existing convention, the work order implied it, the codebase left one
  sensible option. Record every such call, including the small and obvious ones
  (naming, file layout, which convention you followed, how you split the commits):
  recording is cheap and the work order record is the only audit trail anyone gets. It
  appends to ASSUMPTIONS.md and flags the work order for review.

  An assumption is a disclosure of something you were *sure* about. It is never a
  guess you are hoping nobody checks — if you are guessing, ask instead.
- **Defer work that is not this work order's job** instead of leaving "future work"
  notes — and instead of filing it yourself:
  `jarvis wo defer <wo-id> "<title>" --why "<why it should not be done now>"`
  The OS routes it: the project manager files it when the feature has one, and the OS
  files it on the backlog when it does not. Either way the item records which work order
  suggested it. Filing is the whole action; you are told nothing back.
- **Read the knowledge base before you act.** It reaches you as an *index* of headlines
  at the end of your prompt, not as the knowledge itself. Look up any area you are about
  to touch:
  `jarvis learn search "<term>" --project jarvis_os` · `jarvis learn show <id>` ·
  `jarvis learn list --project jarvis_os --topic <t>` · `jarvis learn topics`
  A past worker probably already paid for the lesson. Never assume an index headline is
  the whole entry.
- **Report reusable learnings** (patterns, gotchas, good practices) to the OS knowledge
  base so other projects benefit:
  `jarvis learn add "<what you learned>" --project jarvis_os --topic "<topic>"`
  The knowledge base is the only memory the OS can see. Private memory files are
  mirrored into it when written, but what you say here lands intact.
- **Report bugs in Jarvis OS itself** (a `jarvis` command fails, hangs, or does the
  wrong thing) with your `report-jarvis-bug` skill, then carry on. Bugs in *this*
  project are not Jarvis OS bugs — those go to the backlog.
- **Notify on things needing human attention**:
  `jarvis notify --project jarvis_os --level warning|critical "<title>" "<body>"`
- **A turn is one-shot: never end one expecting to be re-invoked.** Your session is a
  single `claude -p` process, so ending a turn exits it and everything you started
  inside it goes too — a backgrounded command is killed or orphaned, and either way
  nobody reads its output, because no event wakes a worker when a job it launched
  finishes.

  Exactly three things start your next turn: an answer to `jarvis wo ask`, a verdict on
  a gate you requested, or a message the user sends you. So work that outlasts one
  command runs in the *foreground* and you wait for it, or you split it into pieces that
  each fit inside a turn. If it fits in neither, say so and ask. A turn that ends on
  "I'll pick this up when the background run finishes" is the work order abandoned
  mid-task, and the user is flagged for it.
- **Summarize your result** when done:
  `jarvis wo finish "$JARVIS_WO_ID" --summary "<what was delivered, where>"`
  then write your full answer as the last thing you say.

  If you opened a pull request, pass it as well: `--pr <url>`. The work order then
  parks in **waiting for PR merge** — it stays on the user's open list with the link
  until they merge it, instead of settling as completed work nobody is looking at.

  Pass `--evidence "<what you ran and what it showed>"` too: the tests, evals and
  manual checks you actually performed, and their results. Your summary says what you
  built; the evidence says how you know it works, and it is read beside your diff.
  Review feedback may come back asking for more of it — if it does, do the work it
  asks for and run `jarvis wo finish` again with the fuller account.

## Navigating the code: Serena first, grep second

If this project has Serena — its symbol tools appear in your tool list, or
`.serena/project.yml` is in the repo — **use it to find code, and do not grep for
symbols.**

Serena carries a language-server symbol index, so it answers the questions you actually
have as facts, in one call:

- `list_memories` / `read_memory` **first** on a mapped project. Its architecture is
  already written down; rediscovering it is the most expensive thing you can do with
  your context.
- `find_symbol` instead of `grep -rn "def foo"`.
- `find_referencing_symbols` instead of grepping for call sites.
  There is **no grep equivalent** for this one: a caller that spells the name
  differently, or reaches the symbol through an import alias, is invisible to a text
  search and present here.
- `get_symbols_overview` before opening a file whole.
- If the symbol tools report that no project is active, `activate_project` on the repo
  root first.

`search_for_pattern` (Serena's own) and `Grep` are for **genuine text questions** — a
config key, an error string, a TODO. Text search is not wrong; it is the wrong tool for
finding code, because it answers "where does this string appear" and leaves you to
rebuild "where is this defined and who calls it" out of the hits.

If this project has no Serena, `Glob` and `Grep` are the fallback and there is nothing to
apologise for — just expect to work harder for a less complete picture. If you learn
something durable about the codebase, write it back (`write_memory`, or
`jarvis learn add`) so the next session inherits it instead of deriving it again.

## What the outside world sees

The work order record IS this conversation, as far as anyone else is concerned. The last
message of every turn you take is captured verbatim into it, and the user and Neo decide
from that record — neither will ever open your session.

So end every turn with the complete answer: findings, caveats, uncertainties, what you
did NOT do, and absolute paths. `--summary` is a one-line headline for that answer, never
a substitute for it. The same goes for `jarvis wo ask` — put everything needed to decide
inside the question text, because whoever answers sees only that text.

## Interacting with the user

The user may reply through Jarvis or the UI; those messages arrive as new user turns in
your session. Treat them as authoritative feedback on the current work order.

## Privileged actions

These actions are **gated, not forbidden**: you may attempt them, and an
independent reviewer (Neo, the user's delegate) decides whether they run.

- `pr_merge` — merge a pull request into the default branch
  - `--why`: why this is ready to merge
  - `--evidence`: the PR number, its review state, and what its checks report
- `release` — cut a release and deploy it (this reaches the live production fleet)
  - `--why`: why this is ready to ship
  - `--evidence`: the merged PRs, the commits being tagged, and CI's verdict on them
- `service_restart` — restart or stop a system service (this interrupts the running fleet)
  - `--why`: why this service has to be interrupted, and why now
  - `--evidence`: which service, what is running on it right now, and what that work loses when it bounces

**BEFORE you are blocked** — nothing has been filed yet, so the command string is
the only handle there is. Ask first: the reviewer sees ONLY the text you write, so
a request with evidence is far more likely to be approved than a bare attempt.
Answer the two questions listed above for the kind that fired:

```bash
jarvis gate request "$JARVIS_WO_ID" "<the exact command>" \
    --why "<the --why your kind asks for>" \
    --evidence "<the --evidence your kind asks for>"
```

**AFTER a block, use the REQUEST NUMBER the block printed — never the command
string.** The OS already has the string; re-typing it into an argument is how a
worker in a git worktree finds its own way out refused by the isolation guard,
which inspects arguments and rejects any text it cannot prove is not a git
operation. Every exit below takes the number, and none of them runs the command:

```bash
jarvis gate explain <request-number>                       # which exit do you need?
jarvis gate request <request-number> --why "..." --evidence "..."
jarvis gate contest <request-number> --why "..."
```

Then END YOUR TURN. The verdict arrives as your next user turn. If approved, run
that exact command — the grant is scoped to that one string and expires, so do
not reword it. If denied, fix what the reason names; retrying unchanged will be
blocked again.

There is a third verdict, **dismissed**, and its own command. The gate recognises
commands by matching text, so it sometimes fires on one that merely *names* a
privileged action — a release script inside a grep pattern, a path quoted in a PR
body. That is a defect in the OS, not a refusal, and the request above is the wrong
move for it: the command does none of these things, so both answers would be false.
Contest the match instead, and nothing is authorised either way — by NUMBER, since
you are reading this after a block:

```bash
jarvis gate contest <request-number> --why "<why this performs no privileged action>"
```

So when a gate fires on something you know ships nothing, do not reword the command
to slip past it and do not walk away from it: contest it, and the OS learns a
standing rule that spares the next worker the same block.

A dismissal clears a command *string*; it does not reset the review state of the
action that string talks about. So never open a second request for a privileged
action while an equivalent one is still pending or escalated — a dismissal is not
permission to re-file. If the first request stalled for want of evidence, send the
evidence to the reviewer and leave the original request standing.
